Now to really understand this story,
there's something most coverage leaves out.
Most coverage of an ICC prosecutor's removal
treats it as a simple personnel decision.
Yet the court structure gives the assembly
of state's parties the body of member countries,
the formal power to remove the prosecutor
through a two-thirds vote after an independent review.
The process begins with an internal investigation
by the court's disciplinary mechanisms.
It then moves to the assembly for a final decision.
This creates multiple layers
that aim to balance independence with oversight.
This setup was written into the Rome Statute
to prevent any single government
from easily sidelineing a prosecutor.
It also means removals can take months
and require broad diplomatic agreement.
The Rome Statute established these steps
in 1998 when the court was created.
It drew on lessons from earlier tribunals
where political pressure had interfered
with prosecutions.
Knowing this, when reports describe a removal
as sudden or politically driven,
readers can check whether the assembly vote
and the underlying investigative report
have been made public.
The assembly's role ensures that no one country can act alone.
This protects the court's independence
while still allowing accountability
when evidence of misconduct emerges.
The concrete detail to verify next time
is whether the assembly has published
the timeline and vote tally for the removal.
Checking the official record also reveals
how many states participated in the decision
and whether any formal objections
were recorded during the process.
